title: Weather: cold, and another kind of cold
title_target: Погода и времена года — Pogoda i vremena goda
goal: Talk about weather and seasons — Russia's number-one conversation starter — while separating two kinds of "cold" that Russian builds in completely different ways.
bekal: tell холодно (it's cold) and мне холодно (I'm cold) apart
name the four seasons and the months
make natural small talk about the weather

dialogs.title: Диалог — Minus twenty
dialogs.intro: January in Moscow. Ani and Сергей run into each other outside a building. Notice that "cold" shows up in two different patterns, with two different meanings.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Barely. I'm freezing. How many degrees is it?

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.literal: warm?! minus — twenty — two — this — warm?

lines.id: Last week it was minus thirty. Now that was cold.
lines.literal: in — last — week — was — minus — thirty. here — this — was — cold.

lines.id: In Indonesia the lowest temperature is plus eighteen.
lines.literal: in — Indonesia — most — low — temperature — plus — eighteen.

notes: **Холодно without a dative means the weather is cold; with a dative it means a person is cold.** ⚠️ *Сегодня холодно* = it's cold today (a statement about the world). *Мне холодно* = I'm cold (a statement about me). English changes the subject ("it" vs. "I"); Russian adds the dative. The sentence *Я холодный* does exist, but it means "I'm a cold person" — not what you mean.

**Weather sentences have no subject at all.** *Холодно*, *Тепло*, *Жарко*, *Идёт дождь* — there's no "it" or "weather" doing anything. English must slip in *it* ("it's cold"); Russian doesn't: "cold" alone is a full sentence.
**Temperatures below zero are called минус.** *Минус двадцать* (−20). Russia uses Celsius, so −20 °C is about −4 °F. The word **градус** follows the number rule: 1 градус, 2–4 градуса, 5+ градусов.

**Идёт дождь literally means "rain walks."** Russian uses a verb of motion for weather: *Идёт дождь* (it's raining), *Идёт снег* (it's snowing). When it stops: *Дождь кончился*. ⚠️ Don't use падает (falls) — it sounds like something falling off a table.
**Months take в + prepositional, with the ending -е.** *в январ**е***, *в ма**е***, *в июл**е***. Note the stress shifts in some months: январь (yin-VAR') → в январе (v yin-va-RYE).

**Самый + adjective means "the most."** *самая низкая температура* (the lowest temperature), *самый большой город* (the biggest city). Самый changes its ending to match the noun, like any other adjective.

**Weather is Russia's number-one conversation starter, and it's not empty small talk.** In a country where the temperature swings fifty degrees over the year, *Ну и холод сегодня!* (it's freezing today!) is a genuine opener that always works — with neighbors, taxi drivers, or people in line.

rows: It's slippery. ⚠️ the key winter word

after: For the past add **было**, for the future add **будет**: *Вчера **было** холодно*, *Завтра **будет** тепло*. The form is always neuter.
For sentences with a verb (идёт дождь), the past form agrees with the noun: *Шёл дождь* (masc), *Шёл снег* (masc).

grammars.title: Seasons and months
body: Four seasons, twelve months. The right-hand column is the "in that month" form.
after: ⚠️ Months are **not** capitalized in Russian: *в январе*, not *в Январе*. The same rule applies to days of the week and nationalities — all capitalized in English, none in Russian.

Russian months are easy for English speakers to recognize because they come from the same Latin roots: январь/January, февраль/February, март/March. All you need to practice is the stress, which is almost always on the last syllable.

blocks.text: This section isn't in any Russian textbook, but every learner from a warm country who comes to Russia needs it in the first week.

blocks.title: Three things to know in your first Russian winter
items: **A шапка isn't optional.** Russians — especially older women — will scold you in the street if your head is uncovered below zero. The line you'll hear: *Где ваша шапка?!* Take it as a sign of care, because that's what it is.

**Гололёд is more dangerous than мороз.** Sidewalks with a thin layer of ice are the number-one cause of injury for newcomers. The phrase to recognize: **Осторожно, скользко!** — Careful, it's slippery!

**Indoors it's actually very hot.** Russian buildings have central heating that can't be turned off; inside it's often 25 °C (77 °F). That's why people dress in layers: coats come off as soon as you walk in. ⚠️ Walking into someone's home or a classroom with your coat on is considered rude — almost every public building has a **гардероб** (coat check), and using it is mandatory at theaters and museums.
